title: Creating the Big Picture
subtitle: Turn shared direction into useful choices
summary: A big-picture technical leader turns scattered problems into a coherent direction. Vision describes a desired future, strategy describes the coordinated choices to reach it, and written artifacts align people without requiring the staff engineer to become a permanent bottleneck.

concepts.title: Vision
concepts.body: A technical vision describes a coherent future state and why it matters to users and the organization. Describe the future in terms that let people make compatible choices. A useful vision connects the technical landscape to the organization's needs, so it helps people decide what belongs in that future and what should gradually disappear.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A vision says every team can safely evolve the API without a central queue.

concepts.title: Strategy
concepts.body: A strategy is a set of coordinated choices and actions, including what will not be pursued. A vision names a destination; strategy makes choices about reaching it. Account for the starting position, constraints, and priorities. A list of desirable technologies is not enough because it does not resolve competition for people, time, and attention.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A strategy sequences compatibility, migration, and deletion over two quarters.

concepts.title: Alignment
concepts.body: Alignment means affected people share enough context to make compatible decisions without constant escalation. Bring people into the process before presenting a finished answer. Understanding their constraints can change the plan and creates shared ownership. Agreement that a document sounds good is weaker than teams being able to explain how it changes their next decision.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Owners align on one API principle while choosing different implementations.

concepts.title: Writing
concepts.body: Writing creates durable institutional memory and lets readers challenge reasoning asynchronously. Make the audience, purpose, and needed response clear. A written artifact can be reviewed, revisited, and updated as circumstances change. It helps people outside the original conversation see both the proposed direction and the reasoning behind it.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: An RFC preserves the rejected alternatives and the reason for the choice.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Publish a direction
scenario.context: Four teams propose incompatible data APIs. You have one quarter to reduce duplicate work and cannot centralize every implementation decision.

options.label: Write vision and strategy
options.benefit: Clarifies the decision and creates a workable path through the stated constraint.
options.cost: Writing and socializing principles takes time before implementation appears.
options.consequence: A short vision, decision principles, and staged strategy align local designs while leaving teams autonomy.

options.label: Issue a central design
options.benefit: Feels faster or safer in the immediate moment and preserves a familiar habit.
options.cost: Central approval accumulates edge cases and makes the author a gatekeeper.
options.consequence: One design is fast to announce, but teams route every edge case back to you and delivery slows.

scenario.debrief: Both options respond to a real constraint. The stronger choice makes ownership and consequences visible, then creates a point to learn and adjust.

quiz.question: Which statement is a vision rather than a task?
options: Teams can safely ship independent changes
quiz.explanation: A vision describes a coherent future state that can guide many decisions.

quiz.question: What turns a desired future into strategy?
options: Choosing actions and priorities under constraints
quiz.explanation: Strategy makes coordinated choices about reaching the destination.

quiz.question: Why involve affected teams before finalizing a technical direction?
options: Their constraints can improve the plan and its ownership
It removes the need to explain the decision
quiz.explanation: Early participation supplies context and builds shared understanding.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.
